common_name: Delta Snow Garden Phlox (Mildew-Resistant White Purple-Eyed Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing generously for airflow; Delta Snow is a Southern-bred selection valued for consistently strong powdery mildew resistance through humid summers.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, with generous spacing between clumps to maximize air circulation and discourage foliar disease. Delta Snow produces large, fragrant, pyramidal flower trusses of pure white tubular blooms centered with a small purple-pink eye, held on sturdy stems above clean, dark green foliage from midsummer into early fall. Bred in the South for heat and humidity tolerance, it has repeatedly outperformed older white garden phlox cultivars in regional disease trials for its resistance to powdery mildew, making it one of the more dependable tall phlox choices for Gulf Coast borders. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring and deadhead spent trusses to tidy the plant and prevent off-type seedlings from crowding out the named selection.

common_name: Bill Baker Carolina Phlox (Early-Blooming Lilac-Pink Smooth Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Bill Baker forms tidy, non-spreading clumps and flowers about a month earlier than tall garden phlox.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade. Bill Baker is a selection of the mildew-resistant Carolina/smooth phlox complex prized for its lightly fragrant, lilac-pink flower clusters that open in late spring to early summer, roughly a month ahead of the tall garden phlox (Phlox paniculata) cultivars that follow in midsummer. Unlike many woodland phlox species it forms a tidy, clump-forming, non-running habit and holds its glossy, disease-resistant foliage well through the season, earning it the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. Cut back lightly after the main flush to keep plants neat and encourage sporadic rebloom, and divide crowded clumps every three to four years in early spring.

common_name: Red Wings Moss Phlox (Crimson-Red Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Red Wings is a vigorous, mat-forming moss phlox selection grown for its unusually saturated crimson-red flower color.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Red Wings smothers its dense, needle-like evergreen foliage each spring under lightly fragrant, star-shaped crimson-red flowers marked with a darker red eye, a far bolder color than the lavender-blue or white typical of the species. The tight, mat-forming habit knits into a weed-suppressing evergreen carpet ideal for rock gardens, slopes, and wall crevices where sharp drainage keeps the crown dry through winter. Shear lightly immediately after bloom to maintain a dense, compact mat and encourage vigorous new growth, and avoid rich or poorly drained soil, which promotes crown rot and floppy, open growth.

common_name: Scarlet Flame Moss Phlox (Vibrant Scarlet-Red Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Scarlet Flame forms an especially compact, low mat compared with older red moss phlox selections.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Scarlet Flame blankets its dark green, needle-like evergreen foliage in masses of vivid scarlet-red flowers in mid-to-late spring, giving a hotter, more orange-toned red than the deeper crimson of 'Red Wings'. Its especially low, dense, ground-hugging habit makes it well suited to rock gardens, wall tops, and the front edge of sunny borders, where the tight mat suppresses weeds and holds slopes against erosion. Shear lightly after the flush of bloom to keep the mat tight and encourage a fuller second flush of foliage, and ensure sharp drainage since soggy soil quickly leads to crown rot.
